title: Feed the hungry
hookLine: I was hungry and you gave me to eat (Matthew 25:35)
tomorrow: who asks a stranger for a drink, and why does it matter?

lines: THE SMELL REACHES THE DOOR FIRST.
cards: Onions hitting hot oil. Steam off a pot of rice. The smell of a kitchen reaches the front door before you do.

Matthew's Gospel has a king who remembers meals like that. All the nations stand before him, and he tells the ones on his right why they're welcome. In the Douay-Rheims: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat."
They're baffled. Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? And the king answers: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

teach.h: THEY SAW A NEIGHBOR, NOT A KING.
teach.b: So that's when. They never saw a king. They saw a neighbor, a stranger, someone at the door, and they set out a plate.
The meal wasn't sent up to heaven. It went across a table, to one person, and Christ says it reached him there.
The Church gathers this scene into a list.

The Catechism calls the works of mercy charitable actions that help a neighbor in body and in spirit, and it names bodily works: feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and imprisoned, burying the dead.
This block takes them one at a time, starting with the plainest. Notice what the king doesn't ask.
Nobody checks whether the hungry person earned the meal, or how they came to be hungry. Hunger is enough. And notice how ordinary it is.
The just can't even remember the day they did it.
Some readers take that to mean these were everyday meals: a second bowl, a sandwich, groceries left on a step.
Food is the work of mercy you can smell. It's warm, it's shared, and it says, without a speech, you belong at this table.

how: Catholic parishes run food pantries and soup kitchens, and families bring meals to neighbors in need, as one of the corporal works of mercy.

o: give food to someone who has none, without checking
pray before meals for people who are going without
fast once a week so that you feel what hunger is

o: find out his story first so you know he needs it.

games.why: in Matthew 25 nobody checks whether the hungry person earned the meal. hunger is enough, and the king says it reached him.

practice: If there's something to eat or drink nearby, take one slow bite or sip and notice it fully: the smell, the taste, the warmth, the simple fact that it's there.
Then let one person come to mind who may go without a meal today, and keep them company in your thoughts for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Feed the hungry. The first bodily work of mercy in the Catechism's list: food for someone who has none.
